newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Zimbabwe to wait for two weeks for aid decision.
newsitem.headline: Zimbabwe to wait for two weeks for aid decision.

text.p: The World Bank will decide in the next two weeks whether to resume key financial aid for Zimbabwe's economic reforms after reviewing the country's 1997/98 budget, its Harare representative said on Friday.

David Cook told Reuters that on the face of the budget -- a crucial determinant for Western donor aid -- announced on Thursday, the prospects looked good for release of some $62 million of balance-of-payments support the bank withheld in 1995 after Zimbabwe failed to meet some cost-saving targets.

"On the face of it, the prospects are good but we are still reviewing the matter. We are now reviewing the figures (of the budget deficit, gross domestic product (GDP), inflation) in the budget document. We may have to seek clarification on some issues before we make our decision (on resumption of aid)," he said.
"Assuming that this fits the framework of understandings we have with the government, I hope we will be able to make a decision in the next two weeks," he added.

In his budget statement, Finance Minister Herbert Murerwa announced a surprise reduction in the government's spending deficit for the 1996/97 financial year ended June 30 to 7.1 percent of GDP -- not only meeting the government-set target of 8.5 percent but also beating it for the first time in seven years.

The government has, since it embarked on market-led economic reforms in 1991, consistently missed annual targets to whittle down the budget deficit and this was one of the factors that led the World Bank, the IMF and other Western donors to suspend further aid to the southern African country.

Cook said the bank had anticipated that the 1996/97 deficit would "not be too far away from the projections" largely due to increased revenue collections, commerciliasation of loss-making enterprises which had reduced the drain on the fiscus and a Z$1 billion ($867 million) gold payment from the central bank.

Some local economic analysts, including Commercial Bank of Zimbabwe chief economist Danny Dube and Farai Zizhou of the Confederation of Zimbabwe Industries, said the lower deficit was temporary, saying the big central bank payment was just once-off.

They said continuing high government borrowing to finance its expenditure from the domestic market -- forecast as a percentage of GDP at 6.7 percent for the 18 months to December 1998 -- would keep the deficit high.

But Cook said he was encouraged by the government's efforts to control expenditure and urged it to continue streamlining its bloated civil service, carry on with long-delayed privatisation of state firms and strengthen tax collection systems.
"We are encouraged that the government has taken a number of steps already to try to get on top of its fiscal management problems," he said.

"To that extent we are encouraged and positive but that doesn't mean to say one can claim victory yet. If government is able to stay in line with budget forecasts and can achieve its targets then it's on the right path," he said. $1 = Z$11.49
